reason: The cited evidence does not directly address dislocation nucleation barriers at FCC/BCC HEA interfaces under creep. E1 describes room-temperature displacive plasticity in single-phase FCC HEA nanopillars, E3 only describes nanoindentation creep methods without results, and E4 discusses deformation-induced phase transformation in a dual-phase HEA, not interfacial creep in multilayers. The key premises thus lack specific prior support.
premises: Elevated temperature reduces the activation barrier for dislocation nucleation at coherent FCC/BCC HEA interfaces
Sustained loading at elevated temperature leads to progressive build-up of interfacial dislocation arrays and stacking faults
Interfacial dislocation network evolution enables smoother plastic flow and balances strength with deformation tolerance
In situ TEM/STEM can quantitatively map temperature-dependent interfacial dislocation density evolution
